text.p: The following are the main stories from Wednesday morning's German newspapers:
FRANKFURTER ALLGEMEINE ZEITUNG
- Pensions set to rise more in 1996 than they did in 1995, pension fund sources say.
- Row intensifies between Social Democrats and their Green coalition partners in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia.
- Ignatz Bubis, leader of Germany's Jewish community, criticises Switzerland for its behaviour in accepting Nazi gold.
- France and Germany agree broadly on idea of "stability pact" among members of a single European currency.
- East German small and middle-sized business sector still underdeveloped, German Federation of Industry (BDI) says.
HANDELSBLATT
- Deutsche Telekom AG chairman Ron Sommer says his company is ready for privatisation later this year and promises total of 1.5 billion marks in dividends.
- Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer sees room for further capital market interest rate cuts.
- Volkswagen AG presents new working hours plan for its employees.
- IG Metall trade union vows to fight employers' plans to cut sick pay.
SUEDDEUTSCHE ZEITUNG
- More and more employers announce plans to cut sick pay.
- President Roman Herzog cautions against a return to nationalism as 21st century approaches.
- German lawyers accuse the country's highest court, the Consitutional Court, of going beyond its powers.
- Deutsche Telekom uses first half of 1996 to clear off debt in preparation for its floatation later this year.
- German car manufacturers report rise in foreign orders for August but domestic orders were stagnant.
DIE WELT
- Chancellor Helmut Kohl, on visit to Argentina, says he hopes trade between the two countries will increase.
- Row over sick pay threatens to end up in the courts as trade unions consider legal challenge to employers' plans for cuts.
- Kohl expects between five and seven countries to be founder members of a single European currency.
